We have carbon NMR data with chemical shifts. Need to determine number of CH3 groups (methyl). Typically methyl carbon appears around 10-30 ppm for aliphatic, maybe 14 ppm observed. There's a peak at 14.26 ppm, likely a methyl carbon. Also maybe other methyls attached to aromatic? But aromatic methyl (toluene) appears ~21 ppm. Not present. So likely only one methyl group.

Check if any other low-field aliphatic carbon: 61.10 ppm could be a carbon attached to O (e.g., methoxy). That carbon is likely CH3 attached to O (O-CH3) appears ~55-60 ppm. That is also a methyl group (methoxy). So there are two methyl carbons: one at 14.26 (alkyl methyl) and one at 61.10 (methoxy). Both are CH3 groups.

Thus answer 2.

But need to be sure: 61.10 could be a CH2 attached to O? Typically O-CH2 appears ~60 ppm, but CH3-O appears ~55. So could be CH2. However carbon NMR cannot differentiate CH3 vs CH2. Need additional info. Could use proton NMR to see number of methyl protons. Let's get proton NMR.
